title: Simplicial Set
summary: A simplicial set is a contravariant functor from the simplex category to sets. Read the order-preserving maps as operations on simplices, keeping degenerate simplices as part of the data.

references.title: Kerodon — Simplicial Sets
references.author: Jacob Lurie
references.locator: §1.1, Definitions 1.1.0.2 (simplex category), 1.1.0.4 (simplicial object), and 1.1.0.6 (simplicial set; tag 000H)

title: Kan Complex
summary: A Kan complex is a simplicial set in which every horn admits a filler. Check outer as well as inner horns to distinguish this condition from the inner-horn condition for quasicategories.

references.title: Kerodon — Kan Complexes
references.author: Jacob Lurie
references.locator: §1.2.5, Definition 1.2.5.1 (tag 002H), including all horns with n > 0 and 0 ≤ i ≤ n

title: Inner Fibration
summary: Inner fibrations impose the inner-horn lifting condition relative to a map of simplicial sets. Compare left, right, and inner fibrations, then specialize the base to a point to recover the quasicategory condition.

references.title: Higher Topos Theory
references.author: Jacob Lurie
references.locator: Chapter 2, Definition 2.0.0.3 (Joyal), printed p. 53: relative left-, right-, and inner-horn lifting conditions

title: Model Category
summary: Weak equivalences, cofibrations, and fibrations provide an abstract setting for homotopy theory. Riehl expresses the model axioms through two weak factorization systems; unpack their lifting and factorization requirements before using replacements.

references.title: Categorical Homotopy Theory
references.author: Emily Riehl
references.locator: §11.3 Model categories and Quillen functors, Definition 11.3.1, printed p. 138; §§11.1–11.2 Lifting problems and lifting properties / Weak factorization systems

title: Stable Infinity-Category
summary: Stability requires a zero object, fibers and cofibers of every map, and agreement of fiber and cofiber sequences. Begin with spectra, then follow how stable infinity-categories retain the homotopy information behind triangulated categories.

references.title: Higher Algebra
references.author: Jacob Lurie
references.locator: §1.1.1, Definition 1.1.1.9 and Example 1.1.1.11 (spectra); §1.1.2, Remark 1.1.2.16 (relation to triangulated categories)

title: Infinity-Topos
summary: An infinity-topos is an accessible left exact localization of a category of space-valued presheaves on a small infinity-category. Track both accessibility and preservation of finite limits when extending the ordinary topos analogy.

references.title: Higher Topos Theory
references.author: Jacob Lurie
references.locator: §6.1, Definition 6.1.0.4 and Remark 6.1.0.5, printed p. 529 (accessible left exact localization and its size condition)

title: Arzelà–Ascoli Theorem
summary: Uniform boundedness and equicontinuity provide convergent subsequences in spaces of continuous functions on compact domains. Compare this criterion with mere pointwise boundedness to see what controls convergence uniformly.

references.title: Notes on Partial Differential Equations
references.author: John K. Hunter
references.locator: §1.5 Compactness, Theorem 1.14, printed p. 6

title: Radon–Nikodym Theorem
summary: Absolute continuity lets one sigma-finite measure be expressed by integrating a density against another. Read the accompanying Lebesgue decomposition to distinguish this density from the mutually singular part.

references.title: Measure Theory
references.author: John K. Hunter
references.locator: §6.8 Radon-Nikodym theorem, Theorem 6.27 (Lebesgue-Radon-Nikodym theorem)

title: Banach–Alaoglu Theorem
summary: The closed dual unit ball is compact for pointwise evaluation on the original normed space. The separate sequential theorem identifies where separability enters arguments that extract convergent subsequences.

references.title: 245B, Notes 11: The strong and weak topologies
references.author: Terence Tao
references.locator: §3 The weak and weak* topologies, Theorem 3 and Theorem 4 (Sequential Banach-Alaoglu theorem)

title: Rellich–Kondrachov Compactness
summary: On a bounded open domain, bounded families in the zero-boundary-value Sobolev space gain strong subsequential convergence below the critical exponent. Follow the translation estimates that turn derivative control into compactness.

references.title: Notes on Partial Differential Equations
references.author: John K. Hunter
references.locator: §3.10 Compactness results, Theorem 3.45 and its proof, printed pp. 73–75

title: Lax–Milgram Theorem
summary: A bounded coercive bilinear form gives a unique solution for each continuous linear functional. The elliptic application shows how adding a sufficiently large zeroth-order term can restore coercivity.

references.title: Notes on Partial Differential Equations
references.author: John K. Hunter
references.locator: §4.7 The Lax-Milgram theorem and general elliptic PDEs, Theorems 4.20–4.22

title: Pseudodifferential Operator
summary: Pseudodifferential operators extend differential operators through kernels conormal to the diagonal. Follow the bundle-valued kernel construction into ellipticity to connect symbol information with approximate inverses.

references.title: Lectures on Pseudodifferential Operators
references.author: Richard Melrose
references.locator: Chapter 5, §L5.5 Pseudodifferential operators, equation (L5.16), printed p. 55; Chapter 6 Ellipticity, equation (L6.13)

title: CW complex
summary: A CW complex is assembled by attaching disks along their boundary spheres, dimension by dimension. Spheres and projective spaces illustrate how the attaching maps carry information beyond cell counts.

references.title: Algebraic Topology
references.author: Allen Hatcher
references.locator: Chapter 0, Cell Complexes, printed pp. 5–8, including Examples 0.3–0.4

title: cellular homology
summary: Cellular homology computes singular homology using generators indexed by cells. Track how attaching-map degrees determine boundary maps, making a finite CW decomposition into an explicit chain computation.

references.title: Algebraic Topology
references.author: Allen Hatcher
references.locator: §2.2, Cellular Homology, Theorem 2.35 and the following Cellular Boundary Formula

title: cup product
summary: The cup product adds multiplication to cohomology groups. Compare its cochain definition with the surface calculation to see what information survives beyond the ranks of the groups.

references.title: Algebraic Topology
references.author: Allen Hatcher
references.locator: §3.2 Cup Product, cochain definition and Example 3.7, printed pp. 206–207

title: Serre Fibration
summary: Lifting homotopies from disks relates the homotopy groups of a fiber, total space, and base. The long exact sequence extends the lifting viewpoint already familiar from covering spaces.

references.title: Algebraic Topology
references.author: Allen Hatcher
references.locator: §4.2, Fiber Bundles, Theorem 4.41 and the subsequent definition of Serre fibration, printed pp. 375–376

title: Stiefel–Whitney Classes
summary: These mod-two cohomology classes detect features of real vector bundles that survive pullback. Start with the axioms and Whitney sum formula, then relate the classes to obstructions to independent sections.

references.title: Vector Bundles & K-Theory (Version 2.2)
references.author: Allen Hatcher
references.locator: §3.1 Stiefel-Whitney and Chern Classes, Axioms and Construction, Theorem 3.1 (naturality and Whitney sum formula); §3.3 Characteristic Classes as Obstructions

title: Thom Isomorphism
summary: A Thom class shifts cohomology from a vector bundle's base into the relative cohomology of its disk and sphere bundles. Track the orientation hypothesis when moving from mod-two to integer coefficients.

references.title: Algebraic Topology
references.author: Allen Hatcher
references.locator: §4.D Cohomology of Fiber Bundles, Corollary 4D.9 (Thom isomorphism) and Theorem 4D.10 (existence of Thom classes), printed pp. 441–442

title: Quadratic Reciprocity Law
summary: Quadratic reciprocity relates whether one odd prime is a square modulo another to the reversed question. The Legendre symbol and Gauss's lemma turn the sign rule into a method for reducing computations.

references.title: Quadratic Residues, Quadratic Reciprocity, Lecture 9 Notes
references.author: Abhinav Kumar (course instructor; MIT OpenCourseWare)
references.locator: Lecture 9, Legendre Symbol, Lemma 40 (Gauss Lemma), and Theorem 42 (Quadratic Reciprocity Law)

title: p-adic number field
summary: Completing the rationals for the p-adic absolute value produces a field with nonarchimedean convergence. Compute digit expansions before studying its valuation ring and local-field extensions.

references.title: Algebraic Number Theory (v3.08)
references.author: James S. Milne
references.locator: Chapter 7 Absolute Values; Local Fields, Completions, Remark 7.24, Proposition 7.26 (valuation expansions), and Examples 7.27–7.29

title: Hensel's lemma
summary: A simple root over the residue field lifts to a root in a complete discrete valuation ring. Follow Newton's successive corrections, then compare the coprime-factor lifting form of Hensel's lemma.

references.title: Algebraic Number Theory (v3.08)
references.author: James S. Milne
references.locator: Chapter 7, Newton's lemma, Proposition 7.31 (simple-root lifting), and Theorem 7.33 (Hensel's lemma, coprime-factor lifting), printed pp. 120–121

title: Dirichlet's unit theorem
summary: The signature of a number field determines the rank of its unit group. Compare real and imaginary quadratic fields, then follow the logarithmic embedding used to prove finite generation.

references.title: Algebraic Number Theory (v3.08)
references.author: James S. Milne
references.locator: Chapter 5 The Unit Theorem, Theorem 5.1 and the logarithmic-embedding proof

title: Chebotarev Density Theorem
summary: Frobenius conjugacy classes control how often unramified primes exhibit each splitting behavior in a finite Galois extension. Polynomial examples translate the density statement into factorization patterns modulo primes.

references.title: Algebraic Number Theory (v3.08)
references.author: James S. Milne
references.locator: Chapter 8 Global Fields, Chebotarev density theorem, Theorem 8.31 and Example 8.36

title: Borel–Cantelli Lemmas
summary: Summable event probabilities force only finitely many occurrences almost surely. With independence, a divergent sum gives infinitely many occurrences; the repeated-event example explains why that hypothesis cannot simply be omitted.

references.title: Notes on Probability
references.author: Greg Lawler
references.locator: §4 Sums of independent random variables, Lemma 4.3 (Borel-Cantelli Lemma) and the dependent-event counterexample

title: Uniform Integrability
summary: Uniform integrability controls the contribution of large values across a family of random variables. It supplies the extra condition that upgrades convergence in probability to convergence in mean.

references.title: Probability: Theory and Examples (Version 5)
references.author: Rick Durrett
references.locator: §4.6 Uniform Integrability, opening definition and Theorem 4.6.3 (convergence in probability plus uniform integrability versus L1 convergence)

title: Donsker's Invariance Principle
summary: For independent identically distributed increments with mean zero and variance one, rescaled interpolated partial-sum paths converge in distribution to Brownian motion. The path-space statement also controls continuous functionals such as maxima.

references.title: Probability: Theory and Examples (Version 5)
references.author: Rick Durrett
references.locator: §8.1 Donsker's Theorem, Theorems 8.1.2 and 8.1.4 (hypotheses and path-space limit), Example 8.1.6 (maximum), and the proof of Theorem 8.1.4

title: Itô's Formula
summary: Applying a smooth function to Brownian motion introduces a second-derivative correction absent from ordinary calculus. Work through the square-function example to connect that correction with quadratic variation.

references.title: Probability: Theory and Examples (Version 5)
references.author: Rick Durrett
references.locator: §7.6 Itô's formula, Theorem 7.6.1 and Example 7.6.3

title: binomial random graph
summary: Choosing each edge independently gives a graph model in which subgraph counts can be estimated by expectation. The deletion argument converts those estimates into deterministic graphs avoiding a prescribed subgraph.

references.title: Graph Theory and Additive Combinatorics: Exploring Structure and Randomness (author manuscript)
references.author: Yufei Zhao
references.locator: §1.9 Randomized Constructions, opening definition of G(n,p) and Theorem 1.9.1

title: Szemerédi's Graph Regularity Lemma
summary: A bounded partition makes most vertex pairs behave regularly with respect to edge density. The energy-increment proof explains why repeated refinements terminate, despite the rapidly growing number of parts.

references.title: Graph Theory and Additive Combinatorics: Exploring Structure and Randomness (author manuscript)
references.author: Yufei Zhao
references.locator: §2.1 Szemerédi's Graph Regularity Lemma, Theorem 2.1.9 and its energy-increment proof

title: Graphon
summary: A symmetric measurable kernel represents a dense graph limit. Compare step graphons with sampled random graphs, then study how cut distance captures convergence without fixing vertex labels.

references.title: Graph Theory and Additive Combinatorics: Exploring Structure and Randomness (author manuscript)
references.author: Yufei Zhao
references.locator: §4.1 Graphons, Definitions 4.1.1, 4.1.4 and 4.1.5; §4.2 Cut Distance, Definitions 4.2.1 and 4.2.4; §4.4 W-Random Graphs

title: Halting Problem
summary: There is no algorithm deciding whether every encoded machine halts on its supplied input. Follow the diagonal construction carefully: a machine's own description becomes the input that defeats the proposed decision procedure.

references.title: Sets, Logic, Computation: An Open Introduction to Metalogic
references.author: Richard Zach; based on the Open Logic Text by the Open Logic Project
references.locator: §15.3 The Halting Problem, Definition 15.5 and Theorem 15.8 (Unsolvability of the Halting Problem)

title: Löwenheim–Skolem Theorem (Countable Model Form)
summary: In a countable first-order language, a satisfiable theory has a model with at most countably many elements. Skolem's paradox distinguishes an external enumeration from a bijection available inside that model.

references.title: Sets, Logic, Computation: An Open Introduction to Metalogic
references.author: Richard Zach; based on the Open Logic Text by the Open Logic Project
references.locator: §12.11 The Löwenheim–Skolem Theorem, Theorem 12.32 (finite or countably infinite model) and Example 12.34 (Skolem's Paradox)

title: Gödel's First Incompleteness Theorem
summary: A consistent effectively axiomatized theory extending Robinson arithmetic cannot decide every sentence. Compare Gödel's omega-consistency argument with Rosser's refinement to separate the hypotheses used in the two proofs.

references.title: Incompleteness and Computability: An Open Introduction to Gödel's Theorems
references.author: Richard Zach; based on the Open Logic Text by the Open Logic Project
references.locator: §5.3 The First Incompleteness Theorem, Theorem 5.6; §5.4 Rosser's Theorem, Theorem 5.7

title: topological conjugacy
summary: A homeomorphism intertwining two evolution maps transports their orbit structure. Use the defining commuting equation to track periodic points and transitivity, and distinguish this equivalence from a noninvertible factor map.

references.title: Ordinary Differential Equations and Dynamical Systems (author's preliminary version)
references.author: Gerald Teschl
references.locator: §11.3 On the definition of chaos, equation (11.10) and the following discussion of periodic points and transitivity, printed p. 296

title: unique ergodicity
summary: A continuous map of a compact metric space is uniquely ergodic when it has exactly one invariant probability measure. Oxtoby's theorem connects this uniqueness to uniform convergence of continuous-observable time averages.

references.title: MAGIC010 Ergodic Theory, Lecture 6: Continuous transformations of compact metric spaces
references.author: Charles Walkden
references.locator: §6.8 Unique Ergodicity, definition and Theorem 6.11 (Oxtoby's ergodic theorem)

title: topological entropy
summary: Topological entropy measures the exponential growth of orbit segments distinguishable at a fixed resolution. Compare spanning and separated sets before using the variational principle to relate this growth to invariant measures.

references.title: MAGIC010 Ergodic Theory, Lecture 8: Topological entropy
references.author: Charles Walkden
references.locator: §8.4.2 Bowen's definition, spanning/separated-set definitions and Lemma 8.10; §8.5.1 The variational principle, Theorem 8.18
